pronunciation.approximation: KAHR-tih-kay-yah — the first vowel long, e always long in Sanskrit.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit kārttikeya — IAST, with the long ā and the e unmarked (e and o are inherently long in Sanskrit and IAST never macrons them). The restoration Kārttikeya is the correct IAST form; Kārttikēya is a hypercorrection that mistakes the ISO 15919 convention for IAST.

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: Kārttikeya, 'son of the Kṛttikās' — the Pleiades who nursed him, the only major god named for his foster-mothers

domains.title: The Commander of the Gods
domains.subtitle: War, Youth, the Spear, and the Six-Faced One
domains.lead: Kārttikeya is India's god of war at his most beautiful: the six-faced son of Śiva, raised by six star-mothers, who took the spear at seven days old and destroyed the demon no god could touch — and who rides his peacock still through the temples of two nations that call him their own.

cards.name: The Vel
cards.desc: His spear — the lance of victory over the unconquerable, given by his mother and sharp at seven days.

cards.name: The Six Mothers
cards.desc: The Kṛttikās — the Pleiades who found him in the reed-thicket and nursed him, giving him his name.

cards.name: Six Faces
cards.desc: Ṣaṇmukha: the six-faced god who sees every direction at once — the commander's total field of view.

cards.name: The Peacock
cards.desc: His mount — the war-bird that eats serpents, whose dance is also a weapon.

symbols.name: The vel (spear)
symbols.meaning: Focused force — the weapon that ends what the assembled gods could not

symbols.name: The six faces
symbols.meaning: Total sight — the commander who misses nothing on any battlefield

symbols.name: The peacock
symbols.meaning: Pride harnessed to war — beauty made battle-standard

symbols.name: The Kṛttikās, the Pleiades
symbols.meaning: Foster-motherhood raised to the heavens — the stars that named him

symbols.name: The rooster on his banner
symbols.meaning: The war-crow announcing dawn — vigilance that never sleeps

mythology.lead: Kārttikeya's myths are the war-god's perfect résumé: born of fire and stars for one battle, victorious at seven days old, and never outgrown by the cults that made him their own. The Sanskrit epics and Kālidāsa give the north's version; the Tamil Sangam and the Kanda Purāṇam give the south his second, greater career.

myths.title: The Son of Fire and Stars
myths.text: The demon Tārakāsura had ravaged heaven for a thousand years under a boon: only a son of Śiva could kill him — and Śiva sat in ascetic mourning for his dead wife Satī, unmoved by gods, weapons, or time. The gods dispatched Kāma, god of desire, to shoot the ascetic; Śiva burned Kāma to ash with his third eye — and the seed of the awakened god was too hot for any bearer. Agni swallowed it and could not hold it; Gaṅgā took it and laid it in a thicket of reeds (śaravana); there the seed became six infants, found and suckled by the six Kṛttikā stars, the Pleiades (Mahābhārata, Vana Parvan's account of Skanda's birth; Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava 13–15). Pārvatī pressed the six babies into one child with six heads — Ṣaṇmukha. Born of fire, carried by water, raised by stars, and fused by a mother's hands: no single parent could hold him, because every element conspired to make him.

myths.title: Seven Days Old, Commander of the Gods
myths.text: While he was yet a week old, the gods elected the child senāpati — commander-in-chief of the armies of heaven — and his mother gave him the spear, the vel, that is his name and his body in every temple (the Mahābhārata's Skanda cycle; the Purāṇic accounts; Kālidāsa closes the Kumārasambhava with the gods' acclamation, canto 17). At the head of the gods' host he assaulted Tārakāsura's mountain fortress. The demon who had beaten Indra's thunderbolt and every weapon of the pantheon fell to a week-old general with his mother's spear; the thousand-year war ended in a single engagement. The tradition means the arithmetic exactly: the war the adults could not win, the infant finished, because force without freshness is only habit. The war-god who was never young enough to be underestimated is the pantheon's permanent argument that readiness is a decision, not an age.

myths.title: South to Murugan
myths.text: His second great myth is his own migration. The Tamil Sangam anthology praises Murukan — 'the Beautiful' — in the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, one of the earliest long poems in the language, which maps his six hill-abodes (the later Arupadai Veedu) and already knows him as lord of love as well as war. In the south he wooed and won two wives: Devayānai, daughter of Indra, given to him for the Tāraka victory — the court marriage; and Vaḷḷi, the huntress of the hills, won by disguise and persistence in the telling preserved by the Kanda Purāṇam — the mountain marriage. The fuller cycle makes the theology explicit: the Sanskrit war-god and the Tamil hill-god are one, and his household itself marries the two civilizations. The commander who conquered Tāraka's fortress with one spear conquered a whole second civilization without drawing it — conquest by being loved, the one victory his father never managed.

myths.title: Thaipusam and the Kavadi
myths.text: His living myth is the most extreme devotion in Hinduism. The temple legends of Palani tell its charter: Śiva ordered the asura Idumban to carry two hills — Śivagiri and Śaktigiri — slung on a shoulder-pole like a milkman's yoke, from Kailasa to the far south. Resting at Palani, Idumban found the hills suddenly occupied by a child who would not move them back; he fought the boy, fell, and was restored to life and made the guardian of the hill — and the pole-and-burden he carried became the kavadi his devotees still bear. At Thaipusam, at the Kṛttikā-star full moon, millions carry milk-pots and wooden kavadis, some pulling chariots with hooks in their skin, some piercing cheeks and tongues with small spears — the body offered to match the god's gift. From Palani to Sri Lanka's Kataragama to Malaysia's Batu Caves, the war-god's festival is among the largest religious gatherings on earth, and its charter is a demon taught that what the god asks you to carry, he will help you carry.

lore.syncretism: His Tamil identity (Murugan) is the subcontinent's great syncretic achievement: a Sanskrit god fully naturalized in Dravidian soil — the Sangam poems praise him centuries before most Purāṇas were compiled — then exported with Tamil migration to Sri Lanka (Kataragama, where Hindu, Buddhist, and Vedda devotees share one altar), Malaysia, Singapore, Mauritius, South Africa, and Fiji. The Kataragama pilgrimage's multifaith congregation is his unique achievement among the gods: the commander of everyone's armies. In the north he was gradually absorbed by the rising cult of Gaṇeśa — the two sons of Śiva trading popularity century by century — while in the deep south the balance never shifted: Murugan is the most-loved male deity of Tamil Nadu, and his cult never needed to migrate, because the land itself adopted him.
lore.culturalLegacy: Murugan is the most-loved male deity of Tamil Nadu; his six Palani hill-temples are among India's busiest, and Thaipusam at Batu Caves draws well over a million pilgrims annually past a 42.7-metre statue — the tallest Murugan image in the world. His vel decorates everything from Tamil school emblems to the Kataragama flag, and the rooster on his banner announces the hour of worship in a hundred towns. The war-god who was born in a week is also the one who never grew old — the eternal youth of two civilizations, still riding the peacock, his spear still the first word of the Tamil schoolchild's prayer and the last word of the grandmother's blessing.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kārttikeya is the god of arriving exactly as needed. Six mothers, one spear, seven days: nothing in his story wastes a moment. He asks the commander's question, which is also every late-starter's and every young team's: what are you waiting to grow up for — and what would you take on, if you knew you were already enough?

The spear has not dulled: the six hills still fill, the milk-pots still rise, and the Pleiades still rise over Palani in his season, the six star-mothers keeping their appointment with the son. Astronomy and affection never separated in his cult: look up, the stars; look down, the hills; look inward, the spear. The peacock deserves its own line — the war-bird that eats the serpent, dancing at his approach — pride made useful, display made dangerous. His whole household is like that: six mothers, six faces, one spear, zero hesitation. One battle, properly timed, permanently won; and then, like a good commander, letting the calendar do the remembering.

lore.archaeology: His iconography is fixed from the Kushan horizon: the six-headed Shanmukha appears on the coinage of the Yaudheya republic (Punjab-Haryana, ca. 2nd century BCE – 3rd century CE), among the oldest datable named god-images in India. The Palani temples of Tamil Nadu, the Kataragama complex in Sri Lanka, and Malaysia's Batu Caves (272 steps, the world's tallest Murugan statue at 42.7 m) map his living empire. The Yaudheya coinage is the crucial witness: a republic, striking a six-headed god on its money a century and more before most of his temples were built — proof that the commander enlisted human devotees before he had any stone.
